list.listitem: Temporomandibular joint (TMJ) disorders are typically self-limited, and most patients improve over time with or without treatment. C

Self care (avoiding excessive chewing, addressing parafunctional habits, and using relaxation techniques) and noninvasive therapies, such as physical therapy or cognitive behavioral therapy, should be the first choice for treatment. C

An evidence-based guideline (2023) recommends CBT with or without biofeedback, relaxation therapy, manual trigger point therapy, therapist associated mobilization or stretches/exercises for patients with chronic (> 3 months) TMJ pain. B
Temporary and permanent dental occlusal adjustments have not been sufficiently studied to indicate benefit or harm to patients with TMJ disorders. B
Because TMJ disorders can be associated with mental illness or chronic pain syndromes, complicated cases may need to be treated with a multidisciplinary approach. C

background.definition: Temporomandibular disorders include several clinical problems involving the TMJ, masticatory muscles, and associated structures.

list.listitem: As many as one third of adults have at least one symptom of TMJ dysfunction
Women with greater risk of developing TMJ than men, 2:1 ratio
Temporomandibular disorder (TMD) is the second most common musculoskeletal chronic pain disoder, affecting 6-9% of aduls globally
However, at most approximately 5% of adults require treatment for TMJ disorders.
The etiology of TMJ disorders is unclear.
Capsule inflammation and pain may be related to parafunctional habits (eg, teeth clenching, bruxism, and lip biting).
Stress, anxiety, and emotional disturbances often exacerbate symptoms.
A systematic review found only a weak association of bruxism with TMJ, and no association with anterior tooth wear.
There is a strong association between tinnitus and TMJ disorders.
TMJ osteoarthritis is the most common form of arthritis in the jaw and can cause severe pain.
The TMJ contains an articular disc within a synovial capsule and is controlled by the masticatory musculature.
Inflammation of the capsule, microtrauma to the capsular structures, masticatory muscle hyperactivity, or other unrecognized physiology can contribute to the pain of TMJ disorders.
There is no evidence that screening for TMJ disorders is beneficial. C
Joint clicking or popping during mouth opening, pain in the area of the TMJ, and chronic headache may indicate the presence of TMJ syndromes. C
Imaging studies such as CT or MRI are generally not recommended for evaluation. C

Differential.Differential_Features: Visible tooth decay, palpable abscess along gum line
Pain behind posterior molars, tender over emerging tooth
Dull, bulging, and erythematous tympanic membrane
Edema, erythema of external auditory canal, and pain with manipulation of tragus
Fever; tenderness and induration over parotid gland
Induration, tenderness, and erythema over salivary gland
Unilateral, paroxysmal, lancinating pains over trigeminal nerve distribution
Vesicular rash in dermatomal distribution, prodrome of pain, or dysesthesia

list.listitem: The American Academy of Orofacial Pain separates temporomandibular disorders into two main categories, based on anatomical origin of the problem: TMJ disorders and masticatory muscle disorders.
Initial treatment is similar for both types of disorders.
The Fonseca Anamnestic Index (FAI) was found to have accuracy for indentifying pain related and intrarticular TMD. A score of >=25 points is highly accurate for detecting TMD.
Common symptoms of TMJ disorders include painful jaw movement, clicking or grating within the joint, neck pain or stiffness, and headache.
Common signs of TMJ disorders include tenderness over the TMJ, palpable joint clicking or crepitation, flatenning of tooth enamel and limited jaw opening.
A systematic review found a strong association between tinnitus and TMJ disorders.
The ability of diagnostic tests to determine the presence or absence of TMJ disorders has not been adequately studied.
Although CT, arthrography, MRI, and ultrasound are often used to image the TMJ,diagnosis is mainly clinical.
A clinical rule has been proposed but not validated to distinguish between general headache, TMJ disorder, and myofascial pain.
See .

TMJ disorders are generally self-limiting and initial treatment should be focused on self-care instructions (ie, soft diet to avoid excessive chewing, avoid asymmetric chewing, reduce stress, and avoid gum or taffy). C

Although not well studied, noninvasive treatments such as physical therapy modalities, antidepressants, cognitive behavioral therapy, acupuncture, and relaxation techniques should be tried before permanent therapies such as orthodontics and surgery are recommended. C
There is insufficient evidence to show that dental splint therapy provides benefit or harm in patients with TMJ disorders. B

Because TMJ disorders can be associated with mental illness or chronic pain syndromes, complicated cases may need to be treated with a multidisciplinary approach. For patients with >= 3 months of pain, strong recommendation for CBT with or without biofeedback, relaxation therapy, manual trigger point therapy, therapist associated mobilization or stretches/exercises.C
Acetaminophen and NSAIDs are the first choice for treatment of pain. However, studies of pharmacologic interventions for patients with TMJ are generally of low quality.
Muscle relaxants can help with spasm and anxiolytics are an option for spasm or comorbid anxiety disorders, although clinical trials are lacking.
Tricyclic antidepressants are useful for chronic pain treatment.
Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor (SSRIs) may be helpful to treat associated anxiety disorders or depression, but there are case reports of SSRI-induced bruxism.
There is inadequate evidence for effectiveness of management of TMJ osteoarthritis.

For patients with juvenile idiopathic arthritis and TMJ involvement, an initial trial of scheduled NSAIDs and/or intraarticular steroid injection is recommended by American College of Rheumatology guidelines. If response is inadequate, a biologic disease modifying antirheumatic agent (DMARD) and/or methotrexate are recommended.

Surgery is not recommended for uncomplicated TMJ disorders. A systematic review found only 3 clinical trials of orthognathic surgery with inconsistent results of benefit. A subsequent and more extensive meta-analysis identified 23 studies, of which most showed no significant benefit or harm of surgery for TMJ. Arthroscopy may be an option, but there is insufficient evidence to support arthrocentesis and lavage.
There is insufficient evidence to support the use of intra-articular hyaluronate.
A small RCT showed improvement in jaw function, maximal interincisinal opening and jaw pain with intra-articular dextrose injection (prolotherapy)

Intra-articular corticosteroid or anesthetic injection of the TMJ are sometimes recommended used for the treatment of acute symptoms. However, a small RCT showed no benefit from corticosteroid injection with arthrocentesis vs. arthrocentesis alone for TMJ osteoarthritis. Another small RCT (n= 54) found no difference (with improvement in both groups) between corticosteroid and saline injections. Two systematic reviews, including a Cochrane review, concluded that there is a paucity of evidence for corticosteroids for TMJ osteoarthritis.

A small RCT with 24 women compared intra-articular triamcinolone vs placebo solution during arthrocentesis, and reported less chewing pain and a larger mandibular opening at 12 weeks. Given previous negative trials, this should be interpreted cautiously.
Myofascial trigger point injections using local anesthetic may benefit patients with chronic bruxism or acute muscle spasm.
Evidence is uncertain regarding the benefit of arthrocentesis and lavage, based on two small and poor quality clinical trials.
There is insufficient evidence to support occlusal adjustment (adjusting the teeth's biting surfaces).

Temporomandibular total joint replacement implant devices are available. A systematic review of 17 case series with 1343 patients reported generally favorable outcomes for appropriately selected patients refractory to other therapies.

Although none of the following have been well-studied, some options that may help with managing pain include hypnosis, massage, and acupressure. A systematic review found moderate evidence to support the effectiveness of acupuncture compared with placebo or wait list, and similar effectiveness to dental appliances.
Although botulinum toxin has been recommended, clinical trials are lacking and has not been shown to have better outcomes in pain reduction or mouth opening so futher studies are needed.

Low level laser therapy was no more effective than sham therapy in a double-blinded RCT with 40 patients, although both interventions improved symptoms. In another study it was no more effective than occlusal splints.
An evidence-based guideline (2023) recommends manual trigger point therapy, therapist associated mobilization or stretches/exercises for patients with chronic (> 3 months) TMJ pain.
A systematic review found some clinical trial evidence to support the use of active exercises, manual mobilization, and postural training.
Low quality evidence from a systematic review found Cranio Mandibular Manual Therapy (CMMT) can improve pain and maximum mouth opening (MMO) .
A systematic review also found limited evidence to support use of midlaser therapy, iontophoresis, phonophoresis, transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation, and superficial or deep heat.
There is insufficient evidence for splint therapy.
A randomized trial of 60 patients with headache and comorbid TMJ disorder found no benefit of occlusal splints.
A randomized trial of 72 patients wound that pressure release technique (PRT) is found to be effective in reducing pain with patients with chronic TMD
The quality of evidence supporting the following interventions is generally poor but they are low risk and may be helpful: stress management, relaxation techniques, and biofeedback.
An evidence-based guideline (2023) recommends CBT with or without biofeedback and relaxation therapy for patients with chronic (> 3 months) TMJ pain.
A systematic review found 7 trials of cognitive behavioral therapy for chronic orofacial pain; 3 of 4 high-quality trials found short and long-term benefit.
Identify and treat comorbid anxiety disorder or depression.
There is insufficient evidence to show that dental splint therapy provides benefit or harm in patients with TMJ disorders. The same is true of orthodontic interventions.
Avoid gum chewing, wide yawning, singing, and chewy foods, such as taffy.
Eat a soft diet, avoiding solid foods that require a lot of chewing.
Try to chew equally on both sides of the mouth.
Reduce parafunctional habits such as bruxism, cheek biting, excessive chewing, or opening the mouth widely.
Moist heat to the TMJ can help to reduce pain and improve muscle relaxation.

Manual reduction of acute disc displacement: Acute displacement of the intra-articular disc causes the jaw to lock in the open position. Painful inflammation of the articular capsule may limit swallowing and eating, and reduction of the disc displacement should occur urgently.

First, ask the patient to open the mouth wide and move the mandible laterally. If this does not reduce the disc displacement, attempt manual reduction. With the thumb inside the patient's mouth, grasp under the chin. Push down on the posterior teeth and simultaneously pull up on the patient's chin.
Most patients with uncomplicated disease will experience complete resolution of symptoms. C
Approximately 50% of patients improve in 1 year and 85% improve completely by 3 years. C

cell.label: Suspected TMJ disorder: Pain in the area of the TMJ, difficulty chewing, joint clicking or popping, and chronic undifferentiated headache.
Consider urgent treatment with muscle relaxants, oral or IV benzodiazepines.
Proceed immediately to reduction of the dislocated joint, consider IV pain control and/or IV benzodiazepines prior to procedure.
Point tenderness suggestive of a myofascial trigger point?
Consider intramuscular trigger point injection with local anesthetic.
Dental pathology (caries, dental abscess, etc.) on exam?
Infectious etiology causing pain? (Otitis media, otitis externa, parotitis, mastoiditis, and herpes zoster, etc.)
Signs or symptoms suggestive of other pathology?

Recommend self-care for TMJ disorders: rest the masticatory muscles with a soft diet, use NSAIDs or acetaminophen for pain, apply moist heat to the joint for muscle relaxation, and reduce stress and anxiety. Consider referral for other noninvasive therapies such as physical therapy modalities, acupuncture, massage, hypnosis, or stress management. Consider prescription for muscle relaxants, anxiolytics, tri-cyclic antidepressants.
Evaluate and treat the other condition
